newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK - Who's afraid of the CPI?
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK - Who's afraid of the CPI?

text.p: The U.S. benchmark 30-year Treasury bond is likely to remain anchored around a 6-7/8-percent yield with market players cautiously remaining on the sidelines ahead of the September Consumer Price Index on Wednesday, October 16, analysts said.

With the marketplace still divided about the U.S. monetary policy outlook, analysts said an acceleration in the underlying rate of consumer inflation may be the factor eventually prompting the Federal Reserve to tighten credit for the first time since February 1995.
There was no trading in U.S. government securities on Monday due to the Columbus Day holiday. On Friday, the 30-year bond had ended up 16/32 at 98-25 to yield 6.85 percent.

One reason for the bond rally on Friday was the market's perception that wholesale inflation remains relatively well behaved. The core Producer Price Index, however, rose in September by 0.3 percent, partly due to a surge in car prices.
The consensus in a Reuters survey puts both the CPI and its non-energy, non-food core index up 0.3 percent in September -- which would hint at an acceleration in the year-over-year rate.
CS First Boston's chief market strategist Matthew Alexy called the September CPI report "the centerpiece of this week's economic calendar."
"On the margin, it will likely be inflation news which determines both the sizable and not so sizable shifts in market interest rates over the next four trading sessions," Alexy predicted.

Alexy also commented the market is likely to focus on information contributing to third-quarter growth estimates -- meaning the business inventory and merchandise trade reports -- both for the month of August.

"Aside of CPI, most other items will serve the limited purpose of enabling forecasters to fine-tune their third-quarter Gross Domestic Product forecasts," according to Alexy, whose third-quarter GDP growth is up 1.5 percent.
The Fed has repeatedly said it expected the U.S. expansion to slow down in the second half to a non-inflationary pace after rising at an above-trend rate in January-June.

Economists polled by Reuters expect inventories to have risen by 0.3 percent in August and the U.S. international trade balance to have posted an $8.5-billion deficit after a surprisingly large $11.68-billion shortfall in August.
Business inventories are due out on Thursday and the trade data on Friday.
Alexy also predicted that, even if his 1.5-percent forecast underestimated actual third-quarter GDP growth, this may not necessarily be a sign the economy is overheating at an inflationary rate.
"If our up 1.5-percent (GDP) objective is noticeably surpassed, the excess could just as easily portend a drag on October-December production as a building of economic momentum," Alexy concluded.
